1. Restating My Position  
   Nagurski’s candid statements and behavior show that he accepted—and later relinquished—the captaincy purely as a temporary, high-hazard assignment “for a few years,” not out of a desire for permanent authority or reduced stress.  

2. Strong Textual Evidence for a “Temporary Term”  
   A. “I really wanted to relax a little bit more. Besides, the increase in hazard pay was actually more than my salary as a captain… I'm a notch nearer retirement too.” (p. 33)  
     – “Relax” here means returning to the ordinary spaceman’s routine, not seeking less “stress” long-term. He emphasizes pay and “nearing retirement,” implying a time-limited mission.  
   B. “I’ve been in space a good many years… With all due respect, Captain, you must realize that an outsider like you… can never be more than a figurehead.” (p. 31)  
     – He accepts Gavin only because “hazard pay” compensates him for tolerating a rookie, implying the assignment is a paid tour of duty, not a desired promotion.  
   C. Acceptance of Demotion with Relief  
     – When Gavin demotes him back to First Officer, Nagurski offers no protest but immediately helps restore standard procedure, “the way one handles the survey of a planet like this” (p. 35). A man who truly preferred “less stress” would not re-enter dangerous exploration at once.  
   D. Dog Analogy  
     – “The dog or the man who picks his own master is the most content.” (p. 33) Like the dog, Nagurski “chooses” his master and rank for contentment, then moves on when his paid term is up.  

3. Refuting “Less Stress” (Debater_B)  
   A. Hazard Pay Exceeds Captain’s Salary  
     – If Nagurski truly sought lower stress, he would not accept the highest hazard-pay role. His repeated return to exploration under his lower rank shows he values paid exploration over “relaxing” on the ship.  
   B. Risk-Averse Behavior Under “Figurehead” Status, Not Under Full Command  
     – He warns Gavin against “cannibalizing the ship” (p. 35) only when Gavin, the rookie, assumes full command. But he eagerly returns to fieldwork when under experienced or “adult supervision” (p. 44–45). This is not stress avoidance but trust in proven methods.  
   C. No Initiative to Regain Captaincy for Continued “Relaxation”  
     – If his motive were permanent “less stress,” Nagurski would seize any chance to reinstate himself as captain of the restored ship. He does not. Instead, he lets Gavin and the newly indoctrinated Quade lead further exploration, content to remain First Officer.  

4. Logical Consistency of “Tour of Duty” Theory  
   A. Experienced spacemen refer continually to “standard procedure” and “trusted” methods (p. 31, 35), showing they prefer known risks. Only as captain must Nagurski temporarily endure Gavin’s “stupid chances.” Once back under normal leadership, he is “relaxed” again.  
   B. Demotion Example with Quade  
     – Gavin demotes Quade “to Acting Executive Officer” and Quade “hopes I don’t forget” how to “stay alive” (p. 51). Quade, like Nagurski, learned to trust standard methods. Both men show that they willingly give up rank to resume safe, familiar routines once they “learn” the lesson.  

5. Why “Less Stress” Theory Fails  
   A. Disregards Nagurski’s Willingness to “Wade Through Transphasia” (p. 44) when under trusted routine, showing he tolerates known hazards. A man avoiding stress would never volunteer for an exploration “beyond three-mile limit” (p. 37).  
   B. Debater_B’s “stress avoidance” interpretation cannot explain why Nagurski repeatedly returns to exploration parties, uses his “hazard pay,” and enforces “wading through” rather than staying aboard with full shelter. He does the riskiest work only when “paid” and “for a few years.”  

Conclusion  
All evidence—Nagurski’s explicit “relax,” “hazard pay,” and “retirement” motives; his contentment under experienced leadership; his immediate willingness to relinquish rank back to First Officer; and his return to exploration only under “term-limited” assignments—supports the conclusion that he accepted the captaincy only as a temporary tour of duty, not to reduce stress permanently. The “less stress” theory cannot account for his eager returns to high-hazard work and his failure to reassert authority once back under familiar routines.

Before the  tape had cut in, kicked on by the decibel gauge, I had heard or felt  something dark and ominous in the outside air.
